warmup.q: Inside coroutineScope { }, three async calls ask three couriers for a price. One courier throws IOException after 50 ms; the other two would answer at 120 and 300 ms. What does the request get?
options: The lower of the two prices that came back, after 300 ms
The IOException after about 50 ms, and the other two calls are cancelled
The IOException after 300 ms, once the other two calls have finished
Two prices and a null for the courier that failed
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and a plain scope then cancels the other children and rethrows. So the request fails at 50 ms with the IOException, and the two calls that would have answered are cancelled. That's right when you need every answer, and wrong when any one will do. The fix for a price is supervisorScope, this lesson's first change.

opening:
Remember the home cook from the Kotlin coroutines track. When she needed tomatoes, she texted three shops at once and waited only as long as the slowest reply. Now she does it for the post office counter. A customer asks what it costs to send a parcel to Lisbon. She texts three couriers, sets the kitchen timer, and passes on the cheapest reply that came in before it rang.

The plan is simple, and a bad day breaks it in three places. One courier answers with an error, and a careless kitchen throws away the other two replies. One is still typing when the timer rings. And the customer may walk away before anyone answers, leaving three couriers working for nobody.

A Netty server that never blocks its loop left the counter with a promise: quote hands back a ticket at once. In this lesson, we'll keep that promise with coroutines: ask all three couriers together under one deadline, let one fail alone, serve the last good price when nobody answers, and stop the calls when the customer hangs up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook texting three couriers, the kitchen timer running, and a customer who might walk away. Now every request asks all three at once under one deadline. A courier that fails or runs late drops out alone, an old price goes out only with its label, and a hang-up reaches every pot on the stove.

Now look in your own code for coroutineScope around calls where any one answer would do, and for catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } around an await.

Next, we'll put the service under load. What happens when a thousand customers ask at once, and Northline's contract allows only ten calls at a time?

sections.h: One request, three couriers, one deadline
sections.html:
Lesson 1 left the server with a QuoteSource that must return a future at once. This lesson writes that source, in Kotlin. For each request it asks Northline, Eastgate and Fjord for a price, keeps the lowest, and answers by a deadline, whatever the couriers do.

The tool is the coroutine. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding its thread, like a dish the cook leaves to simmer while she starts the next one (Suspend functions from zero). A suspend function is a function that can pause that way. In the lab, each courier is a Provider: a name, and a suspend function quote(destination) that returns that courier's price, or throws.

The shape comes from Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope, where the cook texted three shops first and read the replies after. async starts a coroutine that will bring back a result, and hands you a Deferred, the coroutine's own ticket for that result. awaitAll waits until every ticket has its answer. Say the couriers need 120, 300 and 200 ms. Asked one after another, they take 620 ms. Asked together, they take 300 ms, the time of the slowest:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once
Mono<List<Quote>> allPrices(String destination) {
    return Mono.zip(northline.quote(destination), eastgate.quote(destination), fjord.quote(destination))
            .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
}
Kotlin
suspend fun allPrices(destination: String): List<Quote> = coroutineScope {
    providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(destination) } }   // 1. text all three
        .awaitAll()                                         // 2. then read the replies: the slowest decides
}

coroutineScope gives the three calls a parent that waits for all of them, so none of them can outlive the function. The Java twin uses Reactor from the Reactive track: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once and waits for a value from each, like packing a gift box that closes only when every slot is full.

The deadline is the next decision. A price that arrives after two seconds is no use to a customer standing at the counter. So each call gets the kitchen timer:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: a timeout on each source, turned into "no answer"
Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) {
    return call.timeout(DEADLINE)
            .map(Optional::of)
            .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty()));
}
Kotlin
providers.map { p ->
    async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } }   // null if p misses the deadline
}

withTimeoutOrNull is a cancel with a timer, as Cancellation and timeouts called it. At the deadline it cancels the late call, which stops at its next suspension point, the next place where it pauses, and returns null for it. A deadline is the moment by which the request must answer, whatever its couriers are doing.

You may wonder why each call gets its own timer, and not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out. Both bound the request. Around the whole fan-out, the timer cancels everything and throws away the answers that did arrive. In the figure, Northline answered at 120 ms and Fjord at 200 ms, and with one timer for everything we would still have nothing to say. With a timer per call, only the late courier drops out. Because all the calls start together, a deadline per call is also a deadline for the request.

That's a good day. On a bad day, a courier doesn't just run late. It fails.

sections.h: Let one courier fail alone, and tell your cancel from theirs
sections.html:
The first draft of BestQuote, the starting code of this lesson's lab, uses coroutineScope and withTimeout. Both are wrong for a price, for reasons earlier lessons gave.

coroutineScope treats its children as one unit of work. Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree put it as a kitchen rule: a course goes out only when all of its dishes are ready. So when Northline throws IOException at 50 ms, the scope cancels Eastgate and Fjord and rethrows, as Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers showed with the burnt gravy. That's the right rule when a request needs every answer. A price needs any one of them.

supervisorScope is the bake sale from that lesson, where one burnt tray doesn't spoil the others. Each child fails alone. A failed async keeps its exception in its Deferred, and await hands it to you, where you turn it into "no answer".

withTimeout has a subtler problem. It signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a kind of CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel. Cancellation and timeouts gave the rule: never swallow a CancellationException, or you throw away the message that dinner is off. So you rethrow it, and now one courier's timeout looks like a cancel of the whole request, and ends it.

withTimeoutOrNull turns our own deadline into a plain null. But a courier can still throw a cancellation from deep inside its own code. Fjord's own client has a short fuse: it gives up after 100 ms, and it says so with a TimeoutCancellationException of its own. So we have to be precise, and rethrow only when our coroutine was cancelled. ensureActive() asks exactly that question:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: each source handles its own error, so the zip never sees one
Mono<Optional<Quote>> alone(Mono<Quote> call) {
    return call.map(Optional::of)
            .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty()))   // a failure stays with its courier
            .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty());                 // and so does an empty answer
}
Kotlin
private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? =
    try {
        await()
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()   // 1. were WE cancelled? then this rethrows
        null                                        // 2. no: only the courier's call ended that way
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        null                                        // 3. the courier failed: no answer from it
    }

Let's read the catch in order. If the request itself was cancelled, because the client hung up, ensureActive() throws, and the cancel carries on up (1). If it returns, the cancellation belonged to the courier's call, and that courier simply has no answer (2). Any other exception is a courier that failed, and it counts as no answer too (3).

This section's demo runs the same three calls in three scopes. Northline fails at 50 ms, Fjord's client gives up at 100 ms, and Eastgate answers at 300 ms. On virtual time, a fake clock that skips the waiting, it printed:

Scope Outcome
coroutineScope, awaitAll fails at 50 ms: IOException: northline 503
supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel fails at 100 ms: TimeoutCancellationException
supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel answers eastgate 12.41 at 300 ms

The first scope lost two good couriers to one bad one. The second lost Eastgate's price to Fjord's short fuse. Only the third answered.

A caught cancellation may belong to someone else. Ask whose it is before you rethrow it.

Reactor has no such trap, because there a cancel is not an error signal: you isolate each source with onErrorResume before Mono.zip. The compare block puts the two whole fan-outs side by side.

One courier can now fail alone, and a late one drops out. But what if all three do?

steps: Open FailAloneDemo.kt. Northline fails at 50 ms, Fjord's own client gives up at 100 ms, and Eastgate answers at 300 ms.

Run it. Then, in callAll(), move async { fjord() } to the end of the list and predict the second line again.

code.title: FailAloneDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Deferred import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.ensureActive import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestScope import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.io.IOException import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException // northline fails at 50 ms; fjord's own client gives up at 100 ms; eastgate answers at 300 ms private suspend fun northline(): String { delay(50); throw IOException("northline 503") } private suspend fun fjord(): String = withTimeout(100) { delay(1_000); "fjord 12.43" } private suspend fun eastgate(): String { delay(300); return "eastgate 12.41" } private fun CoroutineScope.callAll(): List<Deferred<String>> = listOf(async { northline() }, async { fjord() }, async { eastgate() }) private suspend fun Deferred<String>.naive(): String? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun Deferred<String>.careful(): String? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun TestScope.attempt(what: String, block: suspend () -> List<String?>) { val t0 = currentTime val outcome = try { "answers ${block()}" } catch (e: Exception) { "failed: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" of ")}" } println("%-40s at %3d ms %s".format(what, currentTime - t0, outcome)) } /** The same three calls in three scopes: who survives a failure, and who survives a timeout? */ fun main() = runTest { attempt("coroutineScope, awaitAll") { coroutineScope { callAll().map { it.await() } } } attempt("supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel") { supervisorScope { callAll().map { it.naive() } } } attempt("supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel") { supervisorScope { callAll().map { it.careful() } } } }

try.expect: coroutineScope fails at 50 ms with the IOException. The naive supervisor fails at 100 ms with TimeoutCancellationException: it rethrew Fjord's timeout as if it were its own cancel. The careful one answers [null, null, eastgate 12.41] at 300 ms. With Fjord last, the naive version waits for Eastgate first, then rethrows Fjord's exception: it fails at 300 ms instead of 100, and still throws Eastgate's price away. The Java twin shows the Reactor side: the raw Mono.zip fails on Northline's error, and with onErrorResume on each call it answers with Eastgate at about 300 ms.

sections.h: When nobody answers, serve the last good price and say it is stale
sections.html:
Sometimes no courier answers by the deadline. The network between us and them is down, or every courier is swamped on the busiest morning of the year. The service then has three choices. It can wait longer, fail the request, or serve the last price it saw.

Waiting longer breaks the deadline, which is the one promise the service makes. Failing is honest, and no help to a customer who only wants a rough idea of the cost. So BestQuote keeps a cache, a store of recent answers kept close at hand: here, the last live price for each destination. When nobody answers, it serves that price marked as stale, old and labelled so, as 7 STALE LISBON 12.41 eastgate. The customer sees the word and decides whether a slightly old price is good enough:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: an empty Optional switches to the cache
.flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination)))
.doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); })   // only live answers refresh the cache
Kotlin
val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price }
if (best != null) {
    cache.remember(best)                       // only live answers refresh the cache
    return best
}
return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale()  // an old price, marked, beats no price
    ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination)     // the handler writes "7 ERR no quote for LISBON"

Two rules keep the cache honest. Only live answers go into it. If a stale answer could refresh the cache, one old price could be served forever, each serving making it look new. And with nothing cached, the request fails with NoQuoteException, which lesson 1's handler turns into 7 ERR no quote for LISBON. A shrug, but at least a quick one. A production cache would also have an age limit, so that a price from a minute ago is served and one from last week is not.

Check yourself: after an outage, the couriers recover. On the next request Eastgate answers 12.39 and Fjord 12.42. What does the customer get, and what does the cache hold for Lisbon afterwards? (OK LISBON 12.39 eastgate, and the cache now holds that live price in place of the old one.)

The fan-out is complete. It still has to meet lesson 1's Java handler, and the handler holds the one thing we haven't used yet: a cancel.

aside.title: Is serving an old price honest?
aside.html: It is when it says so. The reply carries the word STALE, so the customer, or the program they use, knows the price may have moved and can decide. For a rough idea of the cost, a recent price is fine; for a booking, the courier will confirm the real price anyway. What would not be honest is serving the old price as OK. That's why the label lives in the Quote itself, as its stale field, and the protocol turns it into a different word on the wire.

sections.h: Tie each request to its connection with scope.future
sections.html:
Lesson 1's handler calls quote on the event loop, and it cancels the future when the client hangs up. QuoteService connects that future to a coroutine:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: toFuture() subscribes, and cancelling the future cancels the subscription
final class ReactorQuoteSource implements QuoteSource {
    @Override
    public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String destination) {
        return best(destination).toFuture();                         // returns at once; cancel() reaches the zip
    }
}
Kotlin
class QuoteService(context: CoroutineContext, private val best: BestQuote) : QuoteSource, AutoCloseable {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + SupervisorJob())   // 1. owned; failures stay per request

    override fun quote(destination: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> =
        scope.future { best.quote(destination) }                     // 2. returns at once; cancel() reaches it

    override fun close() = scope.cancel()                            // 3. closing the service cancels the rest
}

The service owns a scope, the object that starts coroutines and keeps track of them (1). scope.future { } starts a coroutine in that scope and returns a CompletableFuture at once (2), so the event loop never waits. Coroutines meet Java pictured this bridge as the neighbour's ticket, and here the ticket is tied to the coroutine in both directions. When the coroutine finishes, the future completes. When someone cancels the future, the coroutine is cancelled. Closing the service cancels whatever is left (3).

The second direction is what ties a request to its connection. The client hangs up, channelInactive cancels the future, and the future coroutine is cancelled. The cancel then travels down the job tree, the parent and child links between running coroutines, to the supervisorScope and its three courier calls. The guests have called dinner off, and this time the news reaches every pot on the stove. The picture breaks at the stove, though. A pot comes off the heat the moment the cook lifts it, while a coroutine stops only at its next suspension point, so a courier client stuck in a blocking call keeps going until that call returns (Cancellation and timeouts).

Why not give each connection its own scope and cancel it in channelInactive? That works too, and it's the shape to pick when the handler itself is written in Kotlin. Here, the Java handler from lesson 1 already keeps every pending future and cancels them on close, so a scope per connection would track the same requests twice. With future { }, the Java side holds the ticket, the Kotlin side holds the tree, and neither needs to know how the other works.

Two choices in the scope matter. The scope uses a SupervisorJob, a parent that lets each child fail alone. With a plain Job, one request that fails with NoQuoteException would cancel its parent, and with it every other request in flight. Every later future would then come back cancelled at once. And the scope takes its dispatcher, the part of a coroutine's context that decides which threads run it, as a parameter. Production passes Dispatchers.Default. The tests pass a StandardTestDispatcher, the rehearsal dinner on a fake clock from Shared state and testing coroutines, so every delay and every deadline runs on virtual time, and a test of a 300 ms deadline takes a few milliseconds.

This section's demo starts one request behind scope.future { }, with three courier calls of 300, 400 and 500 ms, and cancels the future after 120 ms, as channelInactive would. All three calls print cancelled within a few milliseconds of the hang-up, and the scope is left with 0 coroutines. The Java twin builds the same request from three supplyAsync calls and cancels it the same way. It prints calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three couriers answer later with nobody listening. Cancelling a plain CompletableFuture voided the ticket and stopped nothing.

A cancel that can't reach the work only hides it. Tie the ticket to the coroutine with future { }.

The service now answers within its deadline and cleans up after a customer who leaves. It still trusts the couriers with as many calls as it likes, and a crowd will test that.

Run it, then run the Java twin, which builds the request from three supplyAsync calls.

code.title: HangUpDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.job import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private val t0 = System.nanoTime() private fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 private suspend fun call(name: String, latency: Long): String = try { delay(latency) println(" $name answered at ${ms()} ms") name } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" $name cancelled at ${ms()} ms") throw e } /** A request coroutine behind a CompletableFuture. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ fun main() { val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + SupervisorJob()) // the service's scope val request = scope.future { // what QuoteService.quote returns supervisorScope { listOf("northline" to 300L, "eastgate" to 400L, "fjord" to 500L) .map { (name, latency) -> async { call(name, latency) } }.awaitAll() } } Thread.sleep(120) println("client hangs up at ${ms()} ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)") request.cancel(true) Thread.sleep(600) println("at ${ms()} ms: coroutines still running in the scope: ${scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count()}") scope.cancel() }

alt.title: HangUpDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent with CompletableFuture: cancel() completes the future, but the calls behind it run on package workbench.quotes.l02; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request built from three supplyAsync calls. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ public class HangUpDemoJava { static final long t0 = System.nanoTime(); static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static String call(String name, long latency) { try { Thread.sleep(latency); System.out.println(" " + name + " answered at " + ms() + " ms, and nobody is listening"); return name; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + " interrupted at " + ms() + " ms"); return null; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> calls = List.of( CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("northline", 300), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("eastgate", 400), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("fjord", 500), pool)); CompletableFuture<List<String>> request = CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(v -> calls.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList()); Thread.sleep(120); System.out.println("client hangs up at " + ms() + " ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)"); request.cancel(true); System.out.println("request cancelled: " + request.isCancelled() + ", calls cancelled: " + calls.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::isCancelled).count() + " of 3"); } // close() waits for the three calls, which finish anyway System.out.println("at " + ms() + " ms: all three calls have finished"); } }

try.expect: All three calls print cancelled within a few milliseconds of the hang-up, and the scope has 0 coroutines left: the cancel went from the future to the coroutine and down to its children. The Java twin reports calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three couriers answer about 300, 400 and 500 ms after the start, with nobody listening. CompletableFuture.cancel completed the outer future and stopped nothing.

compare.title: The fan-out with Reactor's Mono.zip and with coroutines

java.title: BestQuoteReactor.java
java.html: // Reactor: errors, timeouts and empties become values at each source, then Mono.zip Mono<Quote> best(String destination) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northline.quote(destination)), inTime(eastgate.quote(destination)), inTime(fjord.quote(destination))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()) .flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure or a timeout: no answer .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // an empty source would empty the zip } Mono<Quote> fromCache(String destination) { Quote last = cache.lastGood(destination); return last != null ? Mono.just(last.asStale()) : Mono.error(new NoQuoteException(destination)); }

kotlin.title: BestQuote.kt
kotlin.html: class BestQuote( private val providers: List<Provider>, private val deadline: Duration, private val cache: QuoteCache = QuoteCache(), ) { suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { // 1. a failed call doesn't cancel the others providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } } } // 2. late is null, not an exception .map { it.awaitOrNull() } // 3. failed is null too }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) return best } return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination) // 4. stale beats nothing } private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows null // only the provider's call ended that way: no answer } catch (e: Exception) { null // the provider failed: no answer from it } }

compare.note: Both start the three calls together, give each its own deadline, turn a failure into "no answer", keep the lowest price and fall back to the cache. In Reactor, every outcome becomes a value at the source. A timeout is an error signal you resume from, and an empty source is a third outcome you must name with defaultIfEmpty, or Mono.zip completes empty (Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest). Nothing runs until something subscribes, and cancelling the subscription cancels the three calls. In Kotlin, the same policy is ordinary control flow: a scope, try and catch, minByOrNull. The scope guarantees that when quote returns, every call is either done or cancelled. The price of that directness is the CancellationException rule, which only coroutines have: a timeout is a cancel, so you must tell your own cancel from a courier's.

worked.title: Test the deadline and the hang-up on virtual time

steps.say: Make the couriers controllable on the test clock. delay inside runTest uses virtual time, so a fake that delays 1,000 ms costs nothing, and recording cancellations in the catch tells the test exactly who was stopped.
steps.code: class FakeProvider( override val name: String, private val price: String, private val latency: Duration, private val cancelled: MutableList<String>, ) : Provider { override suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { try { delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under runTest } catch (e: CancellationException) { cancelled += name // 2. record who was cancelled throw e } return Quote.live(destination, price, name) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.delay runs on Schedulers.parallel(), which virtual time replaces Mono<Quote> fake(String name, String price, Duration latency, List<String> cancelled) { return Mono.delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under StepVerifier .map(x -> Quote.live("LISBON", price, name)) .doOnCancel(() -> cancelled.add(name)); // 2. record who was cancelled }

steps.say: Test the deadline. currentTime is the virtual clock, so the assertion can be exact: 300, not "under 400". A version on the real clock would take 300 ms per test and could fail on a busy build machine.
steps.code: @Test fun `a provider slower than the deadline is cancelled at the deadline`() = runTest { val best = BestQuote(listOf(northline(120), eastgate(1_000), fjord(200)), deadline = 300.milliseconds) val quote = best.quote("LISBON") assertThat(quote.provider).isEqualTo("fjord") assertThat(currentTime).isEqualTo(300) // 3. exact, and the test takes milliseconds assertThat(cancelled).containsExactly("eastgate") }

steps.say: Test the hang-up through QuoteService. Pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) as its context, and the service's own scope runs on the test clock too. runCurrent() runs what is due now, without moving the clock.
steps.code: @Test fun `cancelling the future cancels all three provider calls`() = runTest { val service = QuoteService(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), slowBest) // 4. inject the test clock val future = service.quote("LISBON") runCurrent() // the three calls have started future.cancel(true) // what channelInactive does runCurrent() assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northline", "eastgate", "fjord") assertThat(service.inFlight).isEqualTo(0) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: cancelling toFuture() cancels the subscription at once CompletableFuture<Quote> future = source.quote("LISBON"); future.cancel(true); // what channelInactive does assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northline", "eastgate", "fjord");

steps.say: Know where virtual time stops. A delay inside withContext(Dispatchers.Default) escapes the test scheduler and takes real time (Shared state and testing coroutines), which is why the service takes its dispatcher as a parameter. The two end-to-end tests in this lab use Dispatchers.Default and a real Netty server, so they assert only with latches: 6 courier calls started, 6 cancelled after the hang-up. Self-check: what would currentTime read in a test that built QuoteService(Dispatchers.Default, ...) inside runTest? (0: the coroutines ran on real threads, and the virtual clock never moved.)

lab.title: Fan out to three couriers, and cancel on hang-up
steps: Run the tests. Ten of eleven fail. The Java files in l02 are lesson 1's solution, carried over; the tests' couriers are in src/test/.../l02/FakeProvider.kt.
Fix BestQuote along points 1 to 3 of its KDoc: supervisorScope, withTimeoutOrNull inside each async, and an await that turns failures into null and rethrows only your own cancel.
Add point 4: remember the best live price, else serve cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale(), else throw NoQuoteException(destination). The six BestQuote tests should pass.

drill.title: Write the best-of fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write BestQuote.quote(destination) from memory: all couriers at once, the same deadline for each, a failed or late courier counts as no answer, your own cancel still propagates, the lowest price wins, and with no answer you serve the cached price as stale or throw NoQuoteException. Which line would break the request when a courier's own client times out?

answer.html: suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } } } .map { d -> try { d.await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null } catch (e: Exception) { null } } }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) return best.also { cache.remember(it) } return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor Mono<Quote> best(String destination) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northline.quote(destination)), inTime(eastgate.quote(destination)), inTime(fjord.quote(destination))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE).map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); }

recap: Fan out with async inside a scope: three couriers at 120, 300 and 200 ms answer in 300 ms instead of 620.
Give each call the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull. A late courier drops out as null and the others still count; one timeout around the whole fan-out throws away answers that already arrived.

supervisorScope lets each courier fail alone, and a courier's own timeout is a CancellationException too. In the catch, currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() rethrows only if your coroutine was cancelled.
With no answer, serve the last live price marked STALE, or fail with NoQuoteException. Only live answers refresh the cache.

scope.future { } gives the Java handler a future at once, and cancelling it cancels the request's coroutine and its courier calls. The scope uses SupervisorJob, so one failed request can't cancel the others.
Where today's service stops: every request still goes to every courier at once, with no limit. A thousand requests mean a thousand calls to each courier.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why BestQuote needs supervisorScope, withTimeoutOrNull on every call and that odd ensureActive() in a catch, and what actually stops the courier calls when a client hangs up. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: A price needs any one courier's answer, not all three, so one courier failing must not cancel the others. In a plain coroutineScope, a failed child cancels its siblings at once, so we use supervisorScope, where each async keeps its failure for await and we turn it into no answer. Each call gets the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull: a late courier becomes null and the others still count, and since all calls start together, the request ends by the deadline. withTimeout would be worse, because its TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, and a courier's own client can throw one too. If we rethrew every CancellationException, one courier's timeout would end the request. So in the catch we call ensureActive: it throws only if our own coroutine was cancelled, and otherwise that courier just has no answer. With no answers, we serve the last live price marked stale, or fail with NoQuoteException. On hang-up, lesson 1's handler cancels the future in channelInactive; scope.future links that future to the request's coroutine, so the coroutine is cancelled and the cancel goes down the job tree to the three courier calls. The service's scope uses SupervisorJob, so one failed request can't cancel the rest.

deeper.html:
Four refinements a production fan-out often adds.

Pass the deadline on. The service knows that a request has, say, 180 ms left; the courier doesn't. Many systems that call each other over a network send the time left along with each call, so that the far side can give up too, instead of finishing work nobody will read. With coroutines you compute it from a start time and pass it down; withTimeoutOrNull then wraps the time that is left, not a fixed number.

Answer early when the answer can't get much better. If any price within 10 cents of the lowest seen in the last minute is good enough, the request can return as soon as one such price arrives, and cancel the rest. That is select over the onAwait clauses (Channels, select and pipelines), with the losers cancelled by hand.

Put an age on the cache. Store the time with each price, and refuse to serve one older than a few minutes. Then a long outage ends in a clear error, not in a price from last week.

Mind the await rule. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc notes that await() on a Deferred that someone else cancelled throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. This lesson's ensureActive() check is the documented way to tell the two apart, and it is worth using anywhere you await work you didn't start.

Lesson 3 of this track adds what the fan-out still lacks: a limit on how many calls each courier sees at once, retries for the calls that are safe to repeat, a second call for the slowest courier, and turning work away when the whole service is full.
